title: Governance, Compliance and Medical Device Security
answer: Enablement audits, local models for patient data, device clearance, bias in triage and connected device security.

children.name: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
children.blurb: An AI enablement audit in healthcare is a structured review of how artificial intelligence systems are selected, deployed, and maintained within a clinical or operational setting.

children.name: Local Models for Patient Data
children.blurb: Local models for patient data are machine learning systems deployed within a healthcare organization's own infrastructure, such as hospital servers, workstations, or approved edge devices, so that protected health information does not leave the organization's control.

children.name: Software as a Medical Device
children.blurb: Software as a Medical Device refers to software intended for medical purposes without being part of a hardware medical device.

children.name: Bias in Clinical Triage
children.blurb: Bias in clinical triage covers systematic differences in how automated systems rank urgency, assign acuity scores, or allocate scarce resources such as beds, imaging, or specialist review.

children.name: Security of Connected Medical Devices
children.blurb: Security of connected medical devices covers the protection of networked clinical hardware such as infusion pumps, patient monitors, imaging systems, and implantable devices, along with their supporting software, data flows, and cloud or hospital interfaces.

sections.body: This field covers the practical governance of artificial intelligence in medicine, including audits before deployment, local data handling, regulatory clearance for software, fairness in triage, and security of networked devices. Artificial intelligence is now doing concrete work in these areas: hospitals run enablement audits to check whether a model fits their workflows, local models process patient records without sending them to external servers, regulators review software as a medical device, and security teams monitor connected monitors and pumps. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, which gives a sense of how many systems now fall under these rules. It also records 210 compliance and regulation pages, reflecting the volume of written requirements. This is not theoretical policy discussion; it is the daily work of keeping AI systems safe and lawful in clinical settings.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Some parts are fairly settled, like the basic structure of a pre-deployment audit and the use of local models to reduce data exposure, but others remain open. Software as a medical device clearance is established for many narrow tools, yet the rules still struggle with models that learn or change after approval. Bias in clinical triage is documented but not solved; audits can find disparities, but removing them without losing accuracy is hard. Connected device security is a known problem with many legacy devices that cannot be patched. The site records 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows that accountability for harm is still being tested in courts. Honest limits include the lack of a single accepted standard for fairness and the difficulty of proving that a local model is truly private.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare, which explains the structured review a hospital runs before turning on a model. Local Models for Patient Data then covers the technical option of keeping records on site, which matters for privacy and for audits. Software as a Medical Device moves to the regulatory side, describing how a tool gets cleared and what that clearance does and does not mean. Bias in Clinical Triage narrows the focus to a specific high risk use, showing how unfair outputs can appear in emergency or intake settings. Security of Connected Medical Devices closes the loop by looking at the physical machines that run or feed these models, from infusion pumps to bedside monitors. Together the pages move from internal review to data handling, then to law, then to fairness, and finally to hardware risk.
